title: Planning, part 5: cost allocation - why segment profit is always contested
subtitle: Direct costs, overheads and the allocation basis: when a number decides whose budget gets cut
whyItMatters: The moment a business starts measuring profit by segment or by product line, allocating overheads becomes the most political subject in every planning cycle. A different allocation basis can turn a product line from profitable to loss-making without a single thing changing in the actual operation.
openingQuestion: Why does the choice of overhead allocation basis matter so much?
openingOptions: Because it changes the total profit of the whole business
Because different bases produce different results
Because the cloud provider bills on one single basis only
Because the infrastructure bill must be fully split across teams every month
explanation: The company's total profit does not change at all, whatever the allocation - allocation only re-slices a pie that is already there. But decisions get made on the segment numbers: a unit assigned a lot of overhead looks less efficient, and in a round of budget cuts it is the first candidate. That is why an apparently neutral technical choice drags very real consequences behind it.

diagram.label: Separate out the direct costs first
Pick a basis that reflects actual usage
Publish the basis to every unit

realWorldExample.company: A software company allocating shared platform costs
realWorldExample.description: The costs of a shared server cluster and data platform are allocated across the product teams. Allocate by revenue and the consumer product, with its large revenue, carries most of the cost. Allocate by compute actually consumed and the result reverses substantially, because the consumer product has many requests but each one is light, while the enterprise product runs many heavy reporting jobs. One pool of cost, two bases, two completely different pictures of efficiency - and two different conclusions about which team deserves more investment.

quiz.question: How do direct costs differ from overheads?
options: Direct costs vary with volume while overheads are always fixed
Direct costs are always far larger than overheads in the total
Direct costs are paid in cash while overheads are paid later
Direct costs trace to one unit without any allocation basis
quiz.explanation: This boundary decides which part of the report is fact and which part is the outcome of a choice. The salary of a division's own sales staff is direct; the salary of the HR department is overhead. Some overheads vary with volume and some direct costs are fixed, the relative size of the two pools differs by industry, and both are settled in cash on ordinary terms.

quiz.question: What makes a good allocation basis?
options: It reflects how much the unit actually uses the shared resource
It is the easiest to compute from what the ledger already gives you
It splits overheads evenly across units, which is the fair way
It gives stable results across periods so years can be compared
quiz.explanation: Splitting evenly sounds fair but is usually the most wrong: a three-person unit and a three-hundred-person unit do not use the HR department in the same way. Ease of computation is a convenience rather than a justification, and stability across periods is exactly the wrong property if usage itself has shifted - the basis should follow the resource consumption, not smooth it away.

quiz.question: Why report segment profit both before and after the allocation of overheads?
options: Because the two come from different data systems, so both must be presented
Pre-allocation measures what the unit controls, post-allocation the full contribution
Because the post-allocation number is always more accurate, so the other is only indicative
Because leadership always asks for segment profit presented on both bases
quiz.explanation: Judging a segment manager should rest on the part they control. Deciding whether to keep a whole product line needs the post-allocation number. Neither figure comes from a separate data system, neither is inherently more accurate than the other, and leadership preference is not why the split exists - the two figures exist because they answer two different management questions.

quiz.question: What is the risk of allocating overheads in too much detail?
options: Units lose the ability to check the number allocated to them
Total allocated cost ends up exceeding actual total overhead
Upkeep effort grows fast while no decision actually changes
The result always tilts toward the units with the largest revenue
quiz.explanation: More detailed allocation is only worth doing when it changes some decision. If both approaches lead to the same conclusion, the simpler one wins. Finer detail does not make the numbers less checkable - if anything the opposite - the total allocated always ties back to the actual overhead pool by construction, and the direction of any bias depends on the basis chosen rather than on the level of detail.

quiz.question: Why publish the allocation basis to the units instead of just sending the final number?
options: Because each unit may pick whichever basis suits it best
Because cloud cost tools require the basis recorded for each team
Because publishing the basis lowers the total overhead allocated
Because most disputes come from nobody knowing how the number was built
quiz.explanation: A division head objecting to an allocated number is rarely objecting to its size - they object because they cannot check where it came from. Put the basis on the table and the argument shifts from 'I refuse to accept this' to 'this machine-hours figure is wrong', which is the kind of argument that can be settled, and which occasionally uncovers a genuinely wrong basis.

keyTakeaways: Allocation does not change total profit, but it changes the numbers decisions rest on
Separate the direct costs first - that part is not up for debate
A good basis reflects real usage; splitting evenly is usually the worst choice
Report both before and after allocation: one for judging people, one for deciding about products
Publish the basis - most disputes come from nobody knowing how the number was built

practicePrompt.question: A product line is profitable before overhead allocation but loss-making after it. Should the line be dropped?
options: Drop it, because once the full cost is counted the line is losing money
Not yet: check whether that overhead really goes away if the line goes
Keep it, since it is still profitable before the overhead allocation
Raise the price to cover the overhead being allocated to the line
practicePrompt.explanation: This is the classic trap of cost allocation. If you drop the product line and the head office rent and the executive salaries stay exactly the same, that overhead simply shifts onto the remaining lines - and the business has just given up the pre-allocation profit this line was contributing. The right question is always which costs genuinely disappear.

summary.keyIdea: Allocation re-slices a fixed pie, but decisions get made on those slices
summary.commonMistake: Treating post-allocation profit as objective fact rather than the outcome of a chosen basis
summary.action: On your current segment report, write down which basis each overhead is being allocated on and why.

application.title: What to do
application.message: Take your largest overhead pool and try allocating it on two different bases, say by revenue and by headcount. Compare the two resulting tables: which units change places in the efficiency ranking? That difference is exactly how much your conclusion depends on a technical choice.
application.secondary: If both approaches give the same conclusion, you can relax. If not, the basis needs to be discussed openly before someone uses the number to cut a budget.

sections.text: This lesson sits where technique meets internal politics. The arithmetic is simple; the difficulty is that every choice inside it produces winners and losers.
The three layers of a segment profit report

sections.title: Reading a segment report layer by layer
sections.subtitle: Each layer answers a different management question

concepts.def: What the unit contributes. There is no subjective choice at this level, which makes it the least contested number in the report.
Deducts the costs the unit's own manager can decide about. This is the figure that should be used to assess that manager.
Deducts the allocated overhead on the chosen basis. Use it for decisions about a product or a unit, never for assessing a person.

sections.label: The only question worth asking when considering closing a unit
sections.text: Not whether the unit is profitable or loss-making after allocation, but: if it goes, which costs genuinely disappear from the business? Head office rent, executive salaries and core system costs barely fall when a product line is closed - they simply get reallocated onto what remains. Plenty of closure decisions have reduced total profit for exactly this reason.

sections.title: Should a department that loses money after allocation be closed?

de_xuat.text: The year-end report shows the Internal Tools department losing money after shared costs are allocated. The CFO proposes closing it. You lead the analysis.

choices.label: Support closing it because it loses money after allocation
Ask: if we close it, which costs actually disappear?
Change the allocation basis so the department looks profitable

dong_ngay.text: The department closes, but headquarters rent, core infrastructure and executive pay barely shrink. They are reallocated to the remaining departments, and total profit falls by exactly the contribution the closed department was making.

doi_tieu_thuc.text: Changing the basis only moves cost onto another department. That one now shows a loss, an argument breaks out, and the total does not change. The move looks like analysis but only shifts the burden.

hoi.text: You split the report into three tiers. After direct costs the department is still positive. Core infrastructure and headquarters rent do not go away if it closes. How do you compare the two options?

choices.label: Use the contribution after direct costs to compare keeping with closing
Reallocate shared costs to the remaining departments and see if they still profit

dong_gop.text: You state it plainly: closing removes only the direct costs and loses the positive contribution too. For judging the manager, use the figure after controllable costs. The company keeps the department and decides on the figure that answers the right question.

chia_lai.text: The remaining departments carry more shared cost, total profit is still lower than if you had kept it, and the argument over the allocation basis eats the whole meeting without anyone answering which costs really disappear.

sections.title: One department, three profit tiers tell three stories
sections.caption: Illustrative figures, in millions of VND. Tier one is the least disputed; tier two is for judging the manager; tier three (after allocated shared costs) is for decisions about a product or department, not for judging people.

lines: The post-allocation number is not objective fact, it is the outcome of a choice that ought to be stated out loud.
The final lesson of the stage puts it all together into the monthly working rhythm of an FP&A professional.
